analysis.one_liner: Moves the consumer financial watchdog's funding from the Federal Reserve to annual congressional approval.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the agency is funded by automatic transfers from Federal Reserve earnings, so Congress cannot use the budget to choke it off. This bill would strip that arrangement and instead require Congress to approve the bureau's money every year. Because a hostile Congress could simply decline to fund it, critics described this as a way to shut down the consumer watchdog without ever voting to repeal it. The bill never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, and other financial companies policed by the CFPB would gain, because an agency whose funding must be reapproved by Congress every year is far easier to weaken, defund, or shut down than one funded automatically.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and other regulated financial firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the CFPB's independent funding stream and requires Congress to appropriate its budget annually, giving lawmakers annual leverage over the agency's operations and existence.

The CFPB was created after the 2008 financial crisis as the main federal agency policing consumer financial products, so any mechanism that allows Congress to cut off its funding reduces enforcement pressure on the financial industry.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost if enforcement of rules against predatory lending, fraudulent fees, and unfair practices weakened because the bureau's funding became hostage to annual political fights.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued in good faith that every federal agency should answer to Congress through the regular appropriations process, and that the CFPB's automatic funding is uniquely unaccountable compared with other regulators.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that annual appropriations give a hostile Congress a practical veto over the bureau, since refusing to fund an agency achieves a repeal without an up-or-down vote on its consumer protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument has some surface appeal, but the CFPB is the only major financial regulator funded outside the appropriations process precisely so its budget cannot be used to pressure its enforcement decisions. Moving it under annual appropriations would primarily shift power over consumer protection from an independent agency to whichever party controlled the House Appropriations Committee, with banks as the immediate beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or a trip to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Sean Duffy introduced the bill on March 4, 2015, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill attracted one cosponsor in the House.
The committee never reported the bill, and no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau came out ahead: the bureau's independent Federal Reserve funding survived intact for the rest of the Congress, and banks gained nothing from the attempt to make its budget subject to annual congressional approval.

for.name: Rep. Sean Duffy
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to move CFPB funding into the annual appropriations process.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and the bill drew no Democratic support in the record; it died quietly in committee with minimal backing from either side.

industries.industry: Banks, payday lenders, and consumer financial companies regulated by the CFPB
industries.note: The bill would have made the bureau's budget dependent on annual congressional approval, giving the industry's allies in Congress a practical lever to weaken or defund its enforcement. The industry's gain would come at the direct expense of consumers the bureau polices.

industries.industry: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (its employees and mission)
industries.note: The bill strips the agency's independent funding and subjects its entire existence to yearly appropriations fights, exposing it to the political pressure its design was meant to prevent.
